article_title: Assessment in Team Problem-Solving Exercises in Computing Education
citation: V. Švábenský, J. Vykopal, S. Leelaluk, P. Čeleda, F. Okubo, A. Shimada. (2026). Assessment in Team Problem-Solving Exercises in Computing Education. Proceedings of the 56th IEEE Frontiers in Education Conference (FIE '26). https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.19209v1
title: Openly released TTX assessment resources: PHI exercise definition, research dataset, results, and Python analytical toolset
description: To support community adoption, the authors release materials under a free, public, open-source license: the PHI exercise definition deployable in the free INJECT Exercise Platform, the research dataset from both TTXs usable to research student behavior and task strategies, comprehensive results and visualizations including those omitted from the paper, and the analytical toolset of Python code that processes the dataset and derives the paper's results. These artifacts let researchers and educators adopt or adapt the assessment methods.
requirements: The PHI exercise definition requires the INJECT Exercise Platform to deploy
target_learning_goals: automated team assessment in cybersecurity exercises
examples: The released dataset covers both TTXs with 23 consenting teams from two countries
key_sources: V. Švábenský, J. Vykopal, S. Leelaluk, P. Čeleda, F. Okubo, A. Shimada. (2026). Assessment in Team Problem-Solving Exercises in Computing Education. Proceedings of the 56th IEEE Frontiers in Education Conference (FIE '26). https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.19209

article_title: Assessment in Team Problem-Solving Exercises in Computing Education
citation: V. Švábenský, J. Vykopal, S. Leelaluk, P. Čeleda, F. Okubo, A. Shimada. (2026). Assessment in Team Problem-Solving Exercises in Computing Education. Proceedings of the 56th IEEE Frontiers in Education Conference (FIE '26). https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.19209v1
title: Five-part scope framework for post-exercise automated team assessment in TTXs
description: The article defines its assessment scope through five grounded characteristics: assessment targets teams rather than individuals, since a team is the fundamental unit and succeeds only when members collectively resolve tasks; it is summative, using milestones as predefined checkpoints that serve as indicators of the learning objectives the team has met; it is exercise-specific, relying only on data collected during the TTX to protect privacy; it is post-exercise, delivering instant results within minutes; and it is fully automated, with manual assessment used only as an evaluation benchmark. This framework organizes the study's two methods and their educational purposes, including grading, hot-wash debriefing, and feedback on deviations from expected procedures.
requirements: Milestones must be predefined in the exercise design so they can indicate met learning objectives
constraints: Individual contributions within a team are explicitly outside the scope; verbal within-team communication is out of scope
target_learners: student teams in higher and formal computing education
target_learning_goals: summative assessment of team problem-solving performance
examples: The framework's post-exercise timing motivated methods that deliver results within minutes instead of hours or days
key_sources: V. Švábenský, J. Vykopal, S. Leelaluk, P. Čeleda, F. Okubo, A. Shimada. (2026). Assessment in Team Problem-Solving Exercises in Computing Education. Proceedings of the 56th IEEE Frontiers in Education Conference (FIE '26). https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.19209

article_title: A Semi-Automated System for Generating Dialogue-Based TTS Lessons Using Large Language Models: An Exploratory Study of Educational Potential
citation: Gendo Kumoi, Fumie Watanabe, Tota Suko, Takashi Ishida, Yuko Kuma, Manabu Kobayashi, and Shigeichi Hirasawa. (2026). A Semi-Automated System for Generating Dialogue-Based TTS Lessons Using Large Language Models: An Exploratory Study of Educational Potential. Preprint, under review at IEEE Access. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.12235
title: Nine design principles for TTS-optimized narration scripts plus a five-stage Expert–Novice dialogue pattern
description: The article presents nine optimization strategies for TTS narration scripts (Table 1), including audience specification, difficulty calibration, sentence length control of approximately 30–40 characters, pacing, audio quality considerations, objective expression, linguistic expression of emotion, reading rhythm, and visual coordination with slides. For dialogue mode it specifies a five-stage basic pattern—"Expert introduces a concept → Novice asks a question→ Expert elaborates→ Novice rephrases→ Expert confirms and extends"—with a speech ratio of Expert 7: Novice 3 and approximately 2–3 sentences per utterance, plus five question strategies (Why, How, What-if, association, confirmation).
requirements: Narration scripts must be optimized for the listenability specific to TTS, since human-written scripts tend to use written-language expressions that cause awkward synthesized speech
constraints: The system does not faithfully implement all elements of cognitive apprenticeship; fading is not realized, and the phrase inspired by is used throughout
target_learners: engineering undergraduates (named as possible audience specification)
target_learning_goals: comprehensible narrated lesson video content across subjects
examples: Single-speaker mode follows a structured composition of opening→ introduction→ main content→ reinforcement→ confirmation→ summary→ closing with linguistic emphasis markers
key_sources: Gendo Kumoi, Fumie Watanabe, Tota Suko, Takashi Ishida, Yuko Kuma, Manabu Kobayashi, and Shigeichi Hirasawa. (2026). A Semi-Automated System for Generating Dialogue-Based TTS Lessons Using Large Language Models: An Exploratory Study of Educational Potential. Preprint, under review at IEEE Access. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.12235

article_title: Effectiveness of school-based programs to reduce bullying: a systematic and meta-analytic review
citation: Maria M. Ttofi, David P. Farrington. (2011). Effectiveness of school-based programs to reduce bullying: a systematic and meta-analytic review. J Exp Criminol. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11292-010-9109-1
title: Systematic review corpus of 622 reports yielding 53 program evaluations and 44 meta-analyzable effect sizes
description: The review assembled an evidence corpus by hand-searching all volumes of 35 journals from 1983 to the end of May 2009 and 18 electronic databases, including non-English reports and unpublished work. Of "622 reports concerned with bullying prevention", 89 reports describing 53 different program evaluations were included, and 44 provided calculable effect sizes for bullying or victimization. Evaluations spanned four design types: randomized experiments, before-and-after intervention-control comparisons, other intervention-control comparisons, and age-cohort designs.
requirements: Studies must compare an intervention group receiving an anti-bullying program with a control group that did not receive it
constraints: Nine evaluations (in 12 reports) were excluded from the meta-analysis due to missing values, lack of data, or implausible effect sizes
target_learners: school students in primary and secondary schools
target_learning_goals: reduction of bullying behavior
reduction of peer victimization
examples: Included programs range from the Olweus Bullying Prevention Program evaluations in Norway to the KiVa program, Steps to Respect, and the Sheffield project
key_sources: Maria M. Ttofi, David P. Farrington. (2011). Effectiveness of school-based programs to reduce bullying: a systematic and meta-analytic review. J Exp Criminol. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11292-010-9109-1

article_title: Stimulating Elementary School Students’ Self-Regulated Learning Through High-Quality Interactions and Relationships: A Narrative Review
citation: Niels J. de Ruig, Peter F. de Jong, Marjolein Zee. (2023). Stimulating Elementary School Students' Self-Regulated Learning Through High-Quality Interactions and Relationships: A Narrative Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09795-5
title: Teaching Through Interactions framework: three domains of classroom-level teacher-student interaction quality
description: The review adopts the Teaching Through Interactions (TTI) framework as its organizing model for classroom-level interaction quality, integrating attachment theory and self-determination theory. As the review states, "The TTI-framework includes three broad domains; instructional support, classroom organization, and emotional support (Hamre et al., 2013)." Instructional support covers promoting inquiry, learning formats, quality feedback, and instructional dialogue; classroom organization covers behavior management, routines, and maximizing learning time; emotional support covers positive climate, sensitivity, and regard for student perspectives. The review uses these domains to structure its synthesis of interaction-SRL associations.
requirements: Studies must measure at least one TTI domain of teacher-student interaction quality, typically via the CLASS observation instrument
constraints: The framework addresses classroom-level interactions; dyadic relationship quality is conceptualized separately via closeness, conflict, and dependency
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning components: metacognition, regulation of cognition, motivation, behavior, and emotions
examples: The review coded all 30 included studies' interaction measures against the TTI domains and their CLASS dimensions
key_sources: Niels J. de Ruig, Peter F. de Jong, Marjolein Zee. (2023). Stimulating Elementary School Students' Self-Regulated Learning Through High-Quality Interactions and Relationships: A Narrative Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09795-5

article_title: Teacher coaching in upper secondary school: Examining the effects on teacher–student interaction and student engagement.
citation: Ertesvåg, S. K., Vaaland, G. S., Tvedt, M. S., Virtanen, T. E., Idsoe, T., Panayiotou, M., Lerang, M. S., Sølvik, R. M., & Lerkkanen, M.-K. (2026). Teacher coaching in upper secondary school: Examining the effects on teacher–student interaction and student engagement. Journal of Educational Psychology, 118(1), 118-137. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000986
title: Teaching Through Interactions (TTI) framework: three domains of teacher–student interaction
description: The TTI framework conceptualizes teacher–student interaction as comprising three domains of teacher support: emotional support, classroom organization, and instructional support. Emotional support promotes motivation and security, classroom organization organizes students' behavior, time, and attention, and instructional support comprises teachers' facilitation of learning opportunities. The article states that "TSI can be conceptualized as comprising three domains of teacher support for student development and learning: emotional support, classroom organization, and instructional support," and uses this framework to structure both the INTERACT intervention topics and the outcome measures.
requirements: The domains are grounded in their presumptive salience for social-emotional development, self-regulation and attention, and cognitive development and achievement
target_learning_goals: social and academic learning supported by high-quality teacher–student interaction
examples: The INTERACT coaching cycles addressed emotional support (first), instructional support (second, fourth, and sixth), classroom organization (third), student engagement (fifth), and a repeated topic of own choice (seventh)

Journal of Educational Psychology, 118(1), 118-137. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000986

article_title: The Effect of Using the Creative Reversal Act in Science Education on Middle School Students' Creativity Levels
citation: Tulin KARACA, Ozlem KORAY. (2017). The Effect of Using the Creative Reversal Act in Science Education on Middle School Students’ Creativity Levels. Eurasian Journal of Educational Research 67 (2017) 199-214. http://dx.doi.org/10.14689/ejer.2017.67.12
title: Torrance Tests of Creative Thinking, Figural Form A, as the creativity outcome measure
description: Figural Form A of the Torrance Tests of Creative Thinking (TTCT) was the data collection instrument, comprising three activities: forming pictures, picture completion, and parallel lines (repeated lines). It "yields the fluency, flexibility, originality, and elaboration su bcomponents of creativity scores and the creativity total score." The test was rated by two raters with an inter-rater reliability coefficient of .75. The subdimensions are defined as fluency (creating various ideas in response to an open-ended question), flexibility (different approaches to a problem), elaboration (detailing the proposed idea), and originality.
requirements: Rated by two raters; the article reports an inter-rater reliability coefficient of .75
target_learning_goals: measuring creativity total score and its fluency, flexibility, originality and elaboration subcomponents
examples: Used as pre- and post-test in the quasi-experimental study, with testing included in a six-week schedule
key_sources: Tulin KARACA, Ozlem KORAY. (2017). The Effect of Using the Creative Reversal Act in Science Education on Middle School Students’ Creativity Levels. Eurasian Journal of Educational Research 67 (2017) 199-214. http://dx.doi.org/10.14689/ejer.2017.67.12

citation: Divoll, Kent and Browning, Sandra (2010) "The "Classroom Ticket" to Concept Retention," International Journal for the Scholarship of Teaching and Learning: Vol. 4: No. 2, Article 10. https://doi.org/10.20429/ijsotl.2010.040210
title: Ticket to retention (TtR) technique distinguished from other classroom assessment techniques in four ways
description: The TtR is a new teaching technique that changes classroom assessment techniques so the emphasis is on student retention of concepts. The authors state "The TtR is different from other classroom assessment techniques in four significant ways": specific questions targeting key concepts rather than vague prompts, multiple peer interactions and active learning, supporting the professor as facilitator of learning, and interacting with topics multiple times in multiple modalities in a short time. Students hear, write, state, and hear each answer so concepts are reviewed at least seven times in one session.
requirements: A sheet with three to five target questions aligned to the professor's precise learning objectives
Collection of written responses by the professor for accountability
constraints: The article reports only preliminary data; no pretest and no experimental or control group were part of the study
target_learning_goals: retention of concepts in long-term memory
assessing student learning and professor instruction
examples: Used in two four-week summer courses and three 15-week fall classroom management courses at a southern university
key_sources: Divoll, Kent and Browning, Sandra (2010) "The "Classroom Ticket" to Concept Retention," International Journal for the Scholarship of Teaching and Learning: Vol. 4: No. 2, Article 10. https://doi.org/10.20429/ijsotl.2010.040210

article_title: Learning L2 Pronunciation with a Text-to-Speech Synthesizer
citation: Cardoso, W. (2018). Learning L2 pronunciation with a text-to-speech synthesizer. In P. Taalas, J. Jalkanen, L. Bradley & S. Thouësny (Eds), Future-proof CALL: language learning as exploration and encounters – short papers from EUROCALL 2018. Research-publishing.net. https://doi.org/10.14705/rpnet.2018.26.806
title: TTS input enhancement: features that increase the quantity and quality of L2 pronunciation input
description: The article proposes that text-to-speech synthesizers support L2 pronunciation learning because they "enhance the target input in both quantity and quality" through manipulable features: speed control, multimodal visual presentation with word highlighting, word/phrase repetition, and voice selection for phonetic variability. Learners manipulate the quantity and quality of exposure to target forms, addressing input availability and accessibility problems that make -ed allomorphy difficult to acquire. In the study, the TTS group used these features in listening activities over four weeks.
requirements: Learners engage in listening activities focused on the pronunciation of target forms, manipulating input quantity and quality via the TTS features
constraints: The literature on pedagogical applications of TTS in L2 education is described as still scarce
target_learning_goals: L2 pronunciation of English regular past tense allomorphy (-id, -d, -t)
examples: The TTS Group completed listen-and-fill-in-the-gap and sound categorization activities using the TTS application over a four-week period
key_sources: Cardoso, W. (2018). Learning L2 pronunciation with a text-to-speech synthesizer. In P. Taalas, J. Jalkanen, L. Bradley & S. Thouësny (Eds), Future-proof CALL: language learning as exploration and encounters – short papers from EUROCALL 2018. Research-publishing.net. https://doi.org/10.14705/rpnet.2018.26.806

article_title: Encouraging Sixth-Grade Students' Problem-Solving Performance by Teaching through Problem Solving
citation: Jonathan D. Bostic, Stephen J. Pape, Tim Jacobbe. (2016). Encouraging Sixth-Grade Students' Problem-Solving Performance by Teaching Through Problem Solving. Investigations in Mathematics Learning, Volume 8, Number 3. https://rcml.org
title: Teaching through problem solving (TTPS) as one of three approaches to problem-solving instruction
description: The article situates TTPS within Schroeder and Lester's three approaches: teaching about, for, and through problem solving. "Teaching through problem solving (TTPS) involves teaching mathematics concepts through problem-solving contexts, provides opportunities for students to develop higher-level thinking during mathematical problem solving, and takes place in an inquiry-oriented learning environment." TTPS lessons begin with word problems carrying high cognitive demand, and students must make sense of both the situation and the underlying mathematics. In this study TTPS is defined as an integration of instructor, instructional method, tasks, and learning environment.
requirements: A supportive, inquiry-oriented learning environment with realistic, complex problems and opportunities for student-to-student discourse
constraints: The article states it is not possible to easily separate an intervention's effects attributed to the instructor, instructional method, tasks, and learning environment in classroom-based research
target_learning_goals: problem-solving performance
mathematics content knowledge (rates, ratios, data analysis)
examples: The intervention classroom solved a pizza best-value problem and a music-preference data problem during the month-long unit
key_sources: Jonathan D. Bostic, Stephen J. Pape, Tim Jacobbe. (2016). Encouraging Sixth-Grade Students' Problem-Solving Performance by Teaching Through Problem Solving. Investigations in Mathematics Learning, Volume 8, Number 3. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1094896

article_title: Encouraging Sixth-Grade Students' Problem-Solving Performance by Teaching through Problem Solving
citation: Jonathan D. Bostic, Stephen J. Pape, Tim Jacobbe. (2016). Encouraging Sixth-Grade Students' Problem-Solving Performance by Teaching Through Problem Solving. Investigations in Mathematics Learning, Volume 8, Number 3. https://rcml.org
title: TTPS lesson sequence: homework check, introductory task, individual then collaborative problem work, whole-class discussion, and closure
description: The article describes a recurring lesson structure for TTPS on block schedules. "Lessons in the intervention classroom conducted during block scheduled periods tended to follow this order: (a) check homework, (b) discuss issues related to homework, (c) complete introductory task, (da) individual work on one problem, (db) examine the problem with a partner or in a small group, (dc) discuss the problem with the entire class, and (e) and complete a concluding activity meant to stimulate reflection." Whole-class discussions continued until at least two distinct approaches were shared, and the instructor ended with a synthesis of concepts, models, and analytic techniques.
requirements: Rich tasks with high cognitive demand
posters reflecting classroom process expectations and an agenda
an instructor who probes with questions rather than telling
constraints: Small-group work lasted 15-25 minutes depending on the problem's complexity, and the whole-class discussion usually took 20-25 minutes
target_learning_goals: problem solving
connectedness of mathematical concepts and procedures
examples: Vignettes of a pizza-pricing problem and a music-preference data problem illustrate the sequence
key_sources: Jonathan D. Bostic, Stephen J. Pape, Tim Jacobbe. (2016). Encouraging Sixth-Grade Students' Problem-Solving Performance by Teaching Through Problem Solving. Investigations in Mathematics Learning, Volume 8, Number 3. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1094896

article_title: Teachers' Views about the Teacher Training Program for Gifted Education
citation: Sayı, A. K. (2018). Teachers’ Views about the Teacher Training Program for Gifted Education. Journal of Education and Learning, 7(4). https://doi.org/10.5539/jel.v7n4p262
title: Teacher Training Program for Gifted Education (TTPGE)
description: A 40-hour certificate program for teachers covering “basic pedagogical formation, thinking-critical thinking and creative thinking training for gifted and talented students and the curriculum integration of these trainings.” Its content has three stages — gifted students, creative thinking, and critical thinking — delivered over two weekends by a university professor and an expert, with a booklet and pre-testing at each practice. The aim is to enable teachers to identify gifted children, learn appropriate methods, and prepare enriched and differentiated lesson plans.
requirements: instructors with degrees and field experience in gifted education
pre-testing of participants to analyze readiness and needs
constraints: short-time format was chosen so teachers from other cities could attend and nonattendance prevented
target_learners: kindergarten, elementary and secondary school teachers
target_learning_goals: identifying gifted children
differentiated and enriched course content
integrating thinking skills into curriculum
examples: Day 4 covered creative thinking techniques including brainstorming, SCAMPER, Synectics, Six Hats, and Creative Problem Solving with application
key_sources: Sayı, A. K. (2018). Teachers’ Views about the Teacher Training Program for Gifted Education. Journal of Education and Learning, 7(4). https://doi.org/10.5539/jel.v7n4p262

article_title: An Investigation of the Effectiveness of Online Text-to-Speech Tools in Improving EFL Teacher Trainees' Pronunciation
citation: Gonca Yangın Ekşi & Sabahattin Yeşilçınar. (2016). An Investigation of the Effectiveness of Online Text-to-Speech Tools in Improving EFL Teacher Trainees’ Pronunciation. English Language Teaching, 9(2). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v9n2p205
title: Online text-to-speech websites (imtranslator, ivona, naturalreader) as self-study pronunciation tools
description: The study focused on three text-to-speech websites — "namely, imtranslator, ivona and naturalreader" — described as "user-friendly and deliver speech-to-text technology in different English accents". Trainees received a training session, then used the sites to prepare for a second oral performance assessed with the same weighted speaking rubric. Trainees used them to compare their own pronunciation with model output and to listen to longer self-generated texts.
requirements: A training session to use the text-to-speech websites
Internet access sufficient for effective listening
target_learners: EFL teacher trainees (pre-service English language teachers)
target_learning_goals: English pronunciation, including word stress, basic intonation patterns and flow of speech
examples: Trainees prepared for an oral achievement test using the websites and were assessed with a five-subsection weighted speaking rubric
key_sources: Gonca Yangın Ekşi & Sabahattin Yeşilçınar. (2016). An Investigation of the Effectiveness of Online Text-to-Speech Tools in Improving EFL Teacher Trainees’ Pronunciation. English Language Teaching, 9(2). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v9n2p205

article_title: An Investigation of the Effectiveness of Online Text-to-Speech Tools in Improving EFL Teacher Trainees' Pronunciation
citation: Gonca Yangın Ekşi & Sabahattin Yeşilçınar. (2016). An Investigation of the Effectiveness of Online Text-to-Speech Tools in Improving EFL Teacher Trainees’ Pronunciation. English Language Teaching, 9(2). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v9n2p205
title: Pre- and post-test quasi-experimental procedure using text-to-speech preparation between oral performances
description: The article used "A pre- and post-test quasi-experimental design" in which a weighted speaking rubric with "five subsections (fluency, pronunciation and accent, voca bulary, accuracy, and content)" assessed initial oral performances, trainees then received "a training session to use text-to-speech websites", and the same rubric assessed second performances after preparation. Three raters graded performances to ensure inter-rater reliability, and paired scores were analysed with a dependent samples t-test in SPSS 21.
requirements: A weighted speaking rubric with defined subsections and weights
Three raters to ensure inter-rater reliability
A training session on the tools before the post-test
constraints: Convenience sampling of two course groups
Findings are from a small-scale case study in one Turkish teacher training programme
target_learning_goals: Oral proficiency: pronunciation, accent and fluency
examples: Argumentative topics elicited persuasive talks of about five minutes assessed before and after tool use
key_sources: Gonca Yangın Ekşi & Sabahattin Yeşilçınar. (2016). An Investigation of the Effectiveness of Online Text-to-Speech Tools in Improving EFL Teacher Trainees’ Pronunciation. English Language Teaching, 9(2). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v9n2p205

article_title: Exploring the 'train the trainer' model for delivering Making Every Contact Count (MECC) training at scale: A qualitative study.
citation: Nichol Beth, Rodrigues Angela M., Audsley Sarah, Haste Anna, Tang Mei Yee, Robson Craig, Harland Jill, Haighton Catherine. (2026). Exploring the ‘train the trainer’ model for delivering Making Every Contact Count (MECC) training at scale: A qualitative study. British Journal of Health Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1111/bjhp.70076
title: Train-the-trainer (TtT) cascade model for delivering MECC training at scale
description: The TtT model "involves using a principal trainer to provide training to individuals so that they become MECC trainers, cascading MECC training to those they go on to deliver training to". The article presents it as an established approach proposed as cost-effective, able to deliver training at scale, and sensitive to context through tailoring opportunities. Its success depends on trainers actually cascading training, which the study found often did not occur. The study analysed this model as implemented for MECC across the NENC region of England.
requirements: Trainers must cascade training after attending the TtT programme, upon which the model's success depends
Organizational top-down support extending beyond TtT attendance to enabling cascade with time and resources
constraints: The study focused on the NENC approach to MECC training and the TtT programme, which may limit generalisability of the findings
TtT models often report low cascade rates, with as few as 20% of trainers cascading training according to literature cited
target_learners: Adult staff across health care, local authority, and voluntary and community sectors eligible for MECC TtT training
target_learning_goals: Delivering person-centred behaviour change conversations (MECC) and cascading that training to others
examples: The NENC regional programme trained principal trainers who delivered MECC TtT courses to trainees who were expected to cascade MECC training onward
key_sources: Nichol Beth, Rodrigues Angela M., Audsley Sarah, Haste Anna, Tang Mei Yee, Robson Craig, Harland Jill, Haighton Catherine. (2026). Exploring the ‘train the trainer’ model for delivering Making Every Contact Count (MECC) training at scale: A qualitative study. British Journal of Health Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1111/bjhp.70076

article_title: Translating training to medical practice in trauma care, a literature review.
citation: Haută Alexandra, Iacobescu Radu-Alexandru, Corlade-Andrei Mihaela, Nedelea Paul Lucian, Cimpoeșu Carmen Diana. (2024). Translating training to medical practice in trauma care, a literature review. European Journal of Trauma and Emergency Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00068-024-02548-1
title: Two-branch taxonomy of trauma team training outcome measures: trained team-related versus patient-specific outcomes
description: The review organizes trauma team training evaluation into trained team-related outcomes — team-specific measures such as 'error rates (the appropriate time, the correct order, the correct frequency)' and 'self-reported outcomes such as team performance, collaboration, and knowledge', plus time-related measures such as time to surveys, intubation, CT, and OR — and patient-specific outcome measures of mortality, morbidity, complication rate, and length of stay. It uses this taxonomy to ask whether training effects transfer to patients.
requirements: Time-related measures should be interpreted alongside other criteria because a fast time does not necessarily imply better patient care
constraints: The review states there is so far no optimal measurement of a TTT program's performance and impact on patients
target_learners: multidisciplinary trauma team members (physicians, nurses, paramedics)
target_learning_goals: evaluating whether trauma team training improves resuscitation performance and patient outcomes
key_sources: Haută Alexandra, Iacobescu Radu-Alexandru, Corlade-Andrei Mihaela, Nedelea Paul Lucian, Cimpoeșu Carmen Diana. (2024). Translating training to medical practice in trauma care, a literature review. European Journal of Trauma and Emergency Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00068-024-02548-1

article_title: Video-based e-learning program for schoolteachers to support children of parents with mental illness: a cluster randomized trial.
citation: Kageyama Masako, Matsushita Atsunori, Kobayashi Ayuna, Sakamoto Taku, Endo Yasuhiro, Sakae Setsuko, Koide Keiko, Saita Ryotaro, Kosaka Hiyuka, Iga Satoko, Yokoyama Keiko. (2023). Video-based e-learning program for schoolteachers to support children of parents with mental illness: a cluster randomized trial. BMC Public Health. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12889-023-15426-z
title: Program structure combining Transtheoretical Model stages with Gagné's instructional events for a 30-minute video
description: The program's content structure combined the Transtheoretical Model of health behavior change with Gagné's instruction. Because awareness of these children is low in Japan, the design focused on pre-contemplation and contemplation stages, using "consciousness-raising, emotional arousal, and self-re-evaluation". Gagné's sequence ran from gaining attention, to stating goals, to new knowledge, to a narrative feedback story, to asking participants what they learned and how they would apply it.
requirements: The TTM stage focus presupposes a topic not yet well recognized by the target audience, requiring consciousness-raising before knowledge delivery
target_learning_goals: Attitude and confidence change regarding supporting children of parents with mental illness
examples: Before providing new knowledge, participants were asked "Have you ever met a child like this?" as a self-re-evaluation prompt; storytelling from a grown child served emotional arousal
key_sources: Kageyama Masako, Matsushita Atsunori, Kobayashi Ayuna, Sakamoto Taku, Endo Yasuhiro, Sakae Setsuko, Koide Keiko, Saita Ryotaro, Kosaka Hiyuka, Iga Satoko, Yokoyama Keiko. (2023). Video-based e-learning program for schoolteachers to support children of parents with mental illness: a cluster randomized trial. BMC Public Health. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12889-023-15426-z
